strengths: The antique botanical plates, near-black ground, restrained ochre accent and editorial serif typography form an unusually specific identity for a coastal planting studio.
The plant register is persuasive evidence rather than decoration: seasonal bars, conditions and project reuse make the studio's expertise tangible without garden photography.
The paid £450 first visit is consistently named, priced and explained, giving the site a commercially useful next step.
Mobile plant cards are substantially recomposed, with alternating image-and-copy arrangements and legible full-width feature cards rather than a simple column collapse.
The strongest pages communicate restraint, resilience and regional seriousness in a voice well matched to affluent coastal clients.

defects.detail: The mobile home render repeats footer content, while the Slaughden desktop page repeats the entire £450 conversion panel. These visible assembly failures make the published experience feel insufficiently checked.
Component duplication and the clipped or repeated content visible beneath the desktop Gardens footer break the otherwise disciplined page rhythm and undermine confidence in the system.

Long plant-register sequences become visually monotonous: repeated cards, fine rules and similarly weighted labels provide too few changes of pace, particularly through the middle of the mobile Planting page.
Calls to action are easy to find, but most repeat the same label without addressing hesitation through availability, geographic fit, process timing or what happens after booking.
The invalid email domain and duplicate publishing artifacts noticeably weaken the trust created by the otherwise authoritative writing and detailed plant evidence.
Some mobile footer and lower-page sections leave excessive empty vertical space, and the small all-caps metadata occasionally approaches marginal readability.

The image language is exceptionally suitable, but repeated use of the same plates across register, project summaries and case studies sometimes feels like inventory reuse rather than a newly composed editorial story.

summary: This is distinctive, highly brand-specific work with an excellent central visual idea: the botanical register turns Marram's planting expertise into both identity and proof. It falls short of pass because duplicated conversion/footer sections, clipped lower-page content and uneven mobile pacing are conspicuous production defects in an otherwise strong design.
